name: command
intent: Encapsulate a request as a first-class value - a command object or function that binds a receiver to the action and its parameters - so the request can be parameterised, queued, logged, undone or replayed independently of the code that raised it.
problem: An action is hard-wired at its call site: the code that decides to do something also knows how to do it, so the request cannot be stored, reordered, retried, audited, undone or sent elsewhere. Every variation - the same action with different parameters, the same action in a queue, the inverse of an action for undo - forces edits at every call site instead of one new request value.
context: Interactive applications that need undo/redo or macro recording, job and work-queue systems that run requests later and elsewhere, auditable or replayable workflows where the performed action must be recorded as data, and boundaries where a request has to cross a process or a machine. It applies whenever the request itself can be expressed as a value - a receiver plus parameters - and some invoker can hold it before and after execution.
benefits: Requests become first-class values that can be queued, scheduled, prioritised, logged, serialised, retried and replayed without the caller knowing how or where they run.
Invoker and receiver are decoupled: the invoker knows only an abstract execute operation, the receiver only performs the work, and neither grows when a new action is added.
Undo/redo, macro recording and auditing come from one uniform pair of operations plus a history instead of a bespoke mechanism per action.
Run-time parameterisation: the same invoker can run different actions, the same action with different parameters, and composites assembled from other commands.
Callers and receivers become independently testable - requests can be asserted on as values, and test doubles can record exactly which commands were submitted.
tradeoffs: One type per action plus an invoker and a history: for a handful of trivial operations the structure costs more than calling a method directly.

A command captures its receiver and parameters at creation time; if the receiver is disposed, replaced or mutated before the command runs (queue delay, replay), the captured state is stale and undo restores the wrong thing.

Undo must be designed per command and never guessed: inverse operations are not always exact (irreversible side effects, external systems, generated identifiers), and a partially applied macro command leaves a state that neither execute nor undo describes.
History holds strong references to receivers and their arguments, which leaks memory and can persist sensitive payloads whenever commands are logged or serialised.
Replayed or serialised commands need stable identity, ordering and idempotency, otherwise a redelivered command applies twice or a newer command is applied to an older state.
Extra allocations and one dispatch layer per request, plus invoker-side bookkeeping (enabled state, cancellation, queue limits) that a direct call does not need.

participants.responsibility: Declares the uniform request interface - typically execute() and, where undo, logging or replay is required, undo() or a stable serialisable identifier. The invoker depends on nothing else.

Binds one receiver, the operation to invoke and the parameters of a single request; implements execute() by delegating the work and, when supported, undo() by restoring the receiver's prior state exactly.
Knows how to perform the work. It holds no knowledge of the invoker, nor of when and by whom it will be asked.
Stores, queues, schedules or logs commands and triggers their execution; it never creates commands and knows no concrete command type.
Creates concrete commands, binds them to receivers with the parameters of the moment, and hands them to the invoker.
A command holding a sequence of sub-commands so that execute and undo apply to the whole group as a single history entry.

use_cases: Editors and design tools with undo/redo: every user edit becomes a command, the history is a stack of them, and a saved session can be replayed from its command log.
Job and work queues: background workers take serialised commands (send mail, resize image, run report) and execute them out of process, with retry on failure.
Audit and change logs: the performed action is written down as data - who, what, which parameters - so it can be reviewed, replayed after a crash, or reversed.
Macro recording: user actions are recorded as commands and re-run as one composite command in scripting, keyboard macros and workflow builders.
Menu, toolbar and shortcut binding in UI toolkits: one invoker is parameterised with a request object and can query whether the command is currently applicable.
Remote or deferred execution: a request created locally is serialised, sent to another process, and executed by an invoker that never saw the receiver.

CQRS command side: commands represent intent to mutate domain state; they carry business-rule validation and produce domain events as outcomes, forming the write half of a command-query responsibility segregation architecture.

Event sourcing building block: commands are the input that drives aggregate state transitions; the immutable event log is the durable record from which current state is replayed, enabling temporal queries and complete audit trails.
Transactional messaging: commands wrap database or service calls so that a transaction manager can coordinate commit/rollback across multiple participants without the sender knowing the details.
Reactive streams with back-pressure: command queues absorb burst traffic and allow downstream consumers to apply back-pressure, preventing cascade failures in high-throughput systems.

Serverless command bus: a cloud-native command bus using EventBridge and Step Functions routes commands to domain handlers with built-in retries, compensation and audit tracing across team boundaries.

IDE refactoring engines and language server protocols: each code transformation (rename, extract method, inline variable) is a command that can be previewed, undone, replayed or serialised for collaborative editing sessions.

Robotic process automation (RPA) and workflow builders: user-recorded automation steps are captured as commands and re-executed as composite workflows, with conditional branching, retry and human-in-the-loop checkpoints.
AI agent and chatbot orchestration: each user intent or agent action is modelled as a command with parameters, enabling queuing, priority, retry and audit of LLM-driven actions in production systems.
Financial order management and trading systems: buy/sell orders are commands with idempotency keys, routed to execution venues with retry, partial fill handling and regulatory audit trails.
Multiplayer collaborative editing: concurrent edits are serialised as commands and applied in causal order, enabling real-time co-editing with conflict resolution and replay from a command log.

Qt Undo Framework: every editing action is a QUndoCommand subclass implementing redo()/undo(), a QUndoStack acts as invoker and history with macro grouping and mergeWith() coalescing, and QUndoView renders the stack so selecting an entry navigates the document to that state.

VS Code extension command registry: extensions bind a unique id to a handler with vscode.commands.registerCommand, and the Command Palette, menus, keybindings and other extensions all invoke the same request by id through executeCommand - no invoker ever sees the handler's code or type.

Java Swing Action/AbstractAction: one Action object carries the behaviour plus text, icon, mnemonic and enabled state, and the same instance backs a menu item, a toolbar button and a key binding via setAction/ActionMap, keeping all invokers in sync from one command value.
avoid_when: The action runs once, synchronously, with no queueing, logging, undo or replay requirement: a direct method call is simpler and clearer.
You only need to pass behaviour around: first-class functions, a Runnable/Callable, a delegate or a closure already are the command - do not wrap them in a class hierarchy.
The only requirement is restoring earlier state: Memento/snapshots or a database transaction may be simpler than inventing an inverse for every action.
A framework already supplies the contract and its invoker (WPF ICommand/RoutedCommand, a message bus with command handlers, a task-queue library): register there instead of rebuilding the roles.
Commands would be stateless wrappers around single method calls with no history - the type-per-action cost outweighs the decoupling.
anti_patterns: Command-as-ceremony: a class per operation whose execute() forwards a single call with no state, no history and no inverse - a function value would do less work.
An invoker that knows concrete command types (instanceof/switch over command classes, or constructing them itself), recreating the coupling the pattern removes.
An unbounded history holding strong references to receivers and payloads, turning undo into a memory leak and a secret-leak channel.
Undo that reconstructs state from a guessed inverse rather than the exact previous value, so repeated undo drifts away from the original state.
Commands capturing live references to mutable domain objects and then being queued or replayed long after, applying stale decisions.
Serialised command logs without versions, identity or idempotency, so replay double-applies effects or fails on an old payload.
Decorated commands where cross-cutting decorators (transactions, security) are mixed inconsistently, producing non-deterministic layering.
Confusing commands with queries: commands carry intent and mutate state; queries return data without side effects. Mixing them breaks CQRS and event sourcing.
God commands: over-large command classes that centralise too much logic, making commands hard to test, compose or undo independently.
Reusing command instances across multiple actions: command state (undo snapshot, execution flag) gets overwritten, corrupting history.
Async void commands in C# or equivalent: unhandled exceptions escape into an uncontrolled synchronization context, crashing the application.
Commands that perform read-model updates synchronously inside the command path, coupling the write path to projection logic and preventing independent scaling.
design_principles: Reify the request: turn an action and its parameters into a first-class value that can be passed, stored and reasoned about (encapsulation).
Dependency inversion between invoker and receiver: both depend on the abstract request instead of each other.
Open/closed principle: new requests arrive as new command types or handlers while the invoker and history stay unchanged.
Single responsibility per role: the command knows the action and parameters, the receiver performs the work, the invoker decides when it runs and records it.
Composition over inheritance: macro/composite commands build larger requests from smaller ones instead of a new monolithic operation.
Command-Query Separation (CQS): commands change state and return nothing; queries return state and change nothing. Do not mix intent in a single interface.
best_practices: Keep commands small and dumb: capture the receiver plus the data execute and undo need, and delegate the real work to the receiver.
Make commands self-contained and immutable after construction so they can be queued, serialised and replayed without surprising aliasing.
Design execute and undo as an exact pair and test them as one invariant (apply, undo, compare state) - never let undo guess an inverse.
Bound the history by size, age or memory, and release references when entries expire; never let the undo log pin live receivers forever.
Give persisted or replayed commands a stable identity, a version and an idempotency key so redelivery is safe.
Let the invoker own bookkeeping - queueing, retry, logging, enabled-state queries, macro grouping - so commands and receivers stay focused.
Capture undo state inside execute(), not at construction time: commands may be queued, so the receiver's state at queue time differs from its state at execution time.
Clear the redo stack on a new execute (fresh action erases the redo future) - this is the most common correctness bug in undo/redo implementations.
In macro commands, undo sub-commands in reverse execution order; if later steps depend on earlier ones, undoing out of order corrupts state.
For distributed command queues, release the consumer lock before executing - holding the queue mutex during command execution serialises producers for no benefit and risks priority inversion.
Use command decorators (transactional, security, logging) to add cross-cutting behaviour without polluting command logic; keep the composition explicit and deterministic.
Prefer std::function / lambdas / closures for fire-and-forget deferred execution where no undo, history or serialization is required - avoid the type-per-action overhead.
Coalesce rapid same-kind commands (e.g., keystrokes) into a single logical command, sealing it on pause or focus change, so undo operates at the right granularity.
For server-synced state, model undo as a new forward compensating command (apply the inverse as a fresh action), not a time-travel rewind - local-only state can rewind freely.
Validate command parameters at construction or execution time; fail fast with clear errors rather than letting invalid commands corrupt receiver state.

Use self-configuring commands when the receiver or required data is only known at execution time: the command resolves its dependencies lazily rather than having the client pre-configure them, avoiding coupling between client and concrete command types.

For concurrent command execution, use thread-safe command histories or execute commands in serial queues per aggregate to prevent race conditions on shared receiver state; never assume execute() is called from a single thread.

Standardise a message envelope early in distributed command bus designs: include command identity, version, source, correlation ID and timestamp to improve observability, replayability, governance and schema evolution.

In CQRS command handlers, load the aggregate from its event stream, apply business rules, and append new domain events with optimistic concurrency control using an expected version; keep projections and read-model updates outside the command path.
For high-throughput command queues, use bounded queue depth with back-pressure signalling so producers slow down when consumers are saturated, preventing cascade failures.

Model long-running, cross-aggregate workflows as process managers (sagas) that emit and react to events, not as single commands - commands target a single aggregate's invariants, while sagas coordinate across bounded contexts.
When commands cross process or machine boundaries, include schema version in the envelope and design forward-compatible parsers so older commands remain valid after schema evolution.
Instrument commands with distributed tracing spans (trace ID, span ID) so execution can be tracked end-to-end across async queue consumers and multi-step workflows.

In async command buses backed by message queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS), use consumer-group partitioning so commands for the same aggregate are always processed by the same consumer instance, preserving ordering guarantees.

Prefer weak_ptr or weak references for receivers when command lifetimes may exceed receiver lifetimes (e.g., queued commands referencing disposed UI controls), avoiding dangling pointer crashes on execution.

In event-sourced systems, commands are the input driving aggregate state transitions; the immutable event log is the source of truth - never mutate events, only append compensating events for corrections.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) - Command (Behavioral Patterns chapter).
